usage: Polite way to ask for quiet in a library, cafe, or meeting
Describes lowering your voice so others aren't disturbed
Common reply about a calm, low-key lifestyle
Casual, slightly sharp; 좀 adds mild irritation
examples: 도서관에서는 조용히 해 주세요.
Please keep quiet in the library.
Standard sign and spoken request you hear everywhere
아기가 자니까 조용히 들어오세요.
The baby's sleeping, so come in quietly.
Pairs naturally with action verbs like 들어오다
요즘은 그냥 집에서 조용히 쉬고 있어요.
These days I'm just resting quietly at home.
Natural way to say you're keeping things low-key
nuance: 조용히 is the adverb of 조용하다 and covers both literal quietness of sound and a calm, low-key way of doing things. It works for asking people to lower their voices and for describing a peaceful lifestyle, so it is far more common in speech than the adjective alone. Note the spelling ends in 히, and the meaning shifts gently from 'silently' to 'calmly' depending on context.
mistakes: Spelling it 조용이; the standard form is 조용히 with 히.
Using 조용히 to mean 'secretly' — for doing something on the sly, 몰래 is the right word.

usage: Most common pairing; hands, dishes, vegetables
For wiping surfaces until no dirt remains
깨끗이 비웠어요 = I cleaned my plate
examples: 밥 먹기 전에 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
Wash your hands well before eating.
Everyday hygiene reminder, very natural
이사 가기 전에 집을 깨끗이 치웠어요.
I cleaned the place up thoroughly before moving out.
Common in the move-out / deposit context
설거지를 깨끗이 해 놓을게요.
I'll get the dishes done nice and clean.
-아/어 놓다 = do in advance and leave it
nuance: 깨끗이 is the adverb from 깨끗하다 and means doing something so the result is clean and complete, not just 'in a clean manner.' It is the natural partner for 씻다, 닦다, 청소하다, where it stresses thoroughness. Watch the spelling: it ends in 이, not 히, which trips up many learners and even some natives.
mistakes: Spelling it 깨끗히; the correct adverb is 깨끗이 with 이.
Using 깨끗이 only for surfaces — it also means finishing something completely, as in 깨끗이 잊다 (forget cleanly / put it behind you).

usage: Telling someone not to move or fidget
Asking someone to stop touching or meddling
now that I think about it quietly
examples: 주사 맞을 때 가만히 있어야 해요.
You have to stay still when getting a shot.
Classic clinic instruction
가만히 좀 있어 봐, 내가 해 줄게.
Hold still a sec, I'll do it for you.
Casual, gentle command to stop moving
가만히 생각해 보니 내가 실수했더라고요.
Thinking it over quietly, I realized I'd messed up.
-더라고요 = recalling a realization
nuance: 가만히 has two everyday senses: physically staying still (가만히 있어) and doing something quietly or letting it be (가만히 둬, 가만히 생각하다). The phrase 가만히 두다 means 'leave alone / not interfere,' which is extremely common in daily life. There is also a warning tone in 가만히 안 둬 (I won't let this slide), so context decides whether it sounds gentle or threatening.
mistakes: Translating it only as 'quietly'; 가만히 often means 'without moving' or 'leave it be,' not silence.
Confusing 가만히 두다 (leave alone) with 가만히 있다 (stay still) — the verb changes the meaning.

usage: Most common pairing; documents, orders, contracts
Making sure nothing is left out
examples: 계약서는 사인하기 전에 꼼꼼히 읽어 보세요.
Read the contract carefully before you sign.
Essential advice for leases and contracts in Korea
짐을 꼼꼼히 챙겼는데도 우산을 두고 왔어요.
Even though I packed carefully, I left my umbrella behind.
-는데도 = even though
사장님이 일을 꼼꼼히 가르쳐 주셨어요.
The boss taught me the work thoroughly.
Compliment about careful, detailed guidance
nuance: 꼼꼼히 is the adverb of 꼼꼼하다 and describes doing something with careful attention to every detail, never skipping or rushing. It is a strong positive in Korea, where being 꼼꼼하다 is praised at work and in study. It pairs best with checking, reading, and preparing verbs, and ends in 히.
mistakes: Spelling it 꼼꼼이; the standard adverb is 꼼꼼히 with 히.
Using it for speed; 꼼꼼히 is about thoroughness, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 is contradictory — careful work is usually unhurried.

examples: 시간은 충분히 있으니까 천천히 하세요.
There's plenty of time, so take your time.
Common reassurance to reduce pressure
고기를 충분히 익혀서 드세요.
Cook the meat thoroughly before eating.
익히다 = to cook through; safety tip
그 마음 충분히 이해해요.
I completely understand how you feel.
Warm, empathetic everyday phrase
nuance: 충분히 means 'enough / sufficiently' and reassures that a quantity or degree has been fully met, whether sleep, time, or understanding. In conversation it often softens into 'completely / totally,' as in 충분히 이해해요 or 충분히 가능해요. It is polite and supportive, which is why it shows up constantly when comforting or encouraging someone.
mistakes: Confusing 충분히 (sufficiently) with 완전히 (completely/entirely); 충분히 means 'enough,' not '100%.'
Forgetting it can mean 'easily / readily' in phrases like 충분히 그럴 수 있어요, not just a literal amount.

usage: 분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come
examples: 분명히 여기 뒀는데 안 보여요.
I definitely put it here, but I can't find it.
Super common when something goes missing
다음부터는 분명히 말씀해 주세요.
Please tell me clearly from next time.
Polite request for unambiguous communication
분명히 어제까지 된다고 했잖아요.
You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.
-잖아요 = as you know / reminding
nuance: 분명히 has two linked uses: 'clearly' as in stating something plainly, and 'surely/definitely' as in expressing strong certainty. The second use is everywhere in spoken Korean, especially the frustrated 분명히 ...했는데 (I definitely did X, but...). It sounds confident and a little insistent, so it carries more conviction than the softer 아마 (probably).
mistakes: Confusing 분명히 (definitely, your own certainty) with 확실히, which can also report objective certainty.
Using 분명히 for a mere guess; it claims real confidence, so a hedge like 아마 fits unsure situations.

usage: 확실히 알아보고 알려줄게요 = I'll check for sure
Pinning something down so there's no doubt
examples: 약을 먹으니까 확실히 좀 나아요.
After taking the medicine, I'm noticeably better.
확실히 = you can clearly tell the difference
이건 확실히 해 둬야 나중에 문제가 없어요.
We should settle this clearly so there's no problem later.
확실히 해 두다 = make sure / nail down
새 폰이 확실히 빠르긴 하네요.
The new phone is definitely faster, I'll give it that.
-긴 하다 = admitting a point
nuance: 확실히 means 'certainly / for sure' and, very usefully, 'noticeably' when you can clearly observe a difference (확실히 빠르다, 확실히 낫다). Compared with 분명히, which stresses the speaker's own conviction, 확실히 leans toward objective, verifiable certainty. The set phrase 확실히 하다 / 확실히 해 두다 means to make something definite, common at work and in agreements.
mistakes: Treating 확실히 and 분명히 as identical; 확실히 emphasizes objective certainty, 분명히 your personal conviction.
Overlooking the 'noticeably' sense; 확실히 다르다 means 'clearly different,' not just 'surely different.'

usage: 간단히 먹읍시다 = let's eat something light
examples: 점심은 김밥으로 간단히 때웠어요.
I just grabbed gimbap for a quick lunch.
때우다 = to make do with; very natural
회의는 간단히 끝낼게요.
I'll keep the meeting short.
Polite promise to be brief at work
간단히 말하면 돈이 부족하다는 거예요.
Simply put, the point is there isn't enough money.
간단히 말하면 = in short
nuance: 간단히 is the adverb of 간단하다 and means doing something in a simple, brief, or light way. It is the go-to for eating something quick (간단히 먹다), keeping explanations short, and wrapping things up without fuss. The phrase 간단히 말하면 ('in short') is a handy connector for summarizing.
mistakes: Confusing 간단히 (simply/briefly) with 쉽게 (easily); a task can be done 간단히 yet not be 쉽게.
Using 간단히 for a big, elaborate meal — it implies something light and quick, not a full spread.

usage: Asking for or giving a full explanation
examples: 사용법을 좀 더 자세히 알려 주시겠어요?
Could you explain how to use it in more detail?
-아/어 주시겠어요 = polite request
계약 조건을 자세히 물어봤어요.
I asked about the contract terms in detail.
Smart move when signing anything
자세히 보니까 흠집이 있더라고요.
When I looked closely, there was a scratch.
Useful when checking a product
nuance: 자세히 means 'in detail / closely' and is the natural opposite of 간단히. It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick summary. It is essential for daily life in Korea, where asking 자세히 설명해 주세요 helps you get the specifics on contracts, services, and instructions.
mistakes: Mixing up 자세히 (in detail) with 정확히 (accurately/exactly); detailed is not the same as precise.
Using 자세히 about quantity; it describes thoroughness of explanation or observation, not amount.

usage: A comment made carelessly, often hurtful
examples: 무심코 한 말이 친구한테 상처가 됐어요.
An offhand remark ended up hurting my friend.
Classic context for 무심코
무심코 버튼을 눌렀다가 취소했어요.
I pressed the button without thinking, then canceled.
-았다가 = did, then reversed
무심코 한 행동인데 오해를 샀어요.
It was a thoughtless act, but it caused a misunderstanding.
오해를 사다 = to invite misunderstanding
nuance: 무심코 means doing or saying something absentmindedly, without conscious intent, and it often sets up an unintended consequence. It is the natural opposite of 일부러 (on purpose). You hear it most in apologies and reflections, as in 무심코 한 말 ('something I said without thinking'), acknowledging there was no bad intent.
mistakes: Confusing 무심코 (without thinking) with 일부러 (on purpose) — they are direct opposites.
Using 무심코 for planned actions; it specifically means there was no intention behind it.

english: on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)
usage: I didn't do it on purpose
Going out of your way to see someone
Choosing not to do something on purpose
examples: 일부러 그런 거 아니니까 너무 미안해하지 마세요.
I didn't mean to do it, so don't feel too sorry.
Reassuring after an accident
바쁠 텐데 일부러 와 줘서 고마워요.
Thanks for coming all this way even though you're busy.
Warm thank-you for someone's effort
일부러 매운 걸 골랐어요, 스트레스 풀려고.
I picked something spicy on purpose, to relieve stress.
Shows the 'deliberately' sense
nuance: 일부러 has two everyday meanings: 'on purpose / intentionally,' and 'going out of one's way / specially' to do something kind. The first appears in apologies (일부러 그런 거 아니에요), the second in thanks (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요). Tone and context decide which, but both stress deliberate intent, making it the opposite of 무심코.
mistakes: Confusing 일부러 (on purpose) with 억지로 (reluctantly/forcibly); intent is not the same as being forced.
Missing the warm 'going out of your way' sense, which is very common when thanking someone.

english: to one's heart's content, as much as you like
usage: eat as much as you like
Telling someone to have a great time
to rest as much as you want
examples: 많이 차렸으니까 마음껏 드세요.
I made a lot, so please help yourself.
차리다 = to set out food; warm hospitality
오늘은 시험 끝났으니까 마음껏 놀자.
The exam's over today, so let's have all the fun we want.
마음껏 놀다 = play/hang out freely
휴가 동안 마음껏 쉬다 왔어요.
I rested as much as I wanted during the vacation.
Satisfying way to describe a good break
nuance: 마음껏 means doing something fully and freely, to your heart's content, with no need to hold back. It is a generous, warm word, perfect for hosting (마음껏 드세요) and for encouraging someone to enjoy or rest without restraint. The -껏 ending means 'to the full extent of,' and you will also meet it in 힘껏 (with all one's strength).
mistakes: Writing it as two words 마음 껏; -껏 attaches directly to make 마음껏.
Using 마음껏 where a limit applies — it specifically means freely and without holding back, so it clashes with restrictions.
